newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Dream of cashless society becomes Russia nightmare.
newsitem.headline: Dream of cashless society becomes Russia nightmare.

text.p: Idealists in the Soviet communist era dreamed in vain of a society without cash, where workers received what they needed and goods were available on demand.
The first half of their vision has become a grim reality, five years after the superpower fell apart in a slow, painful transition to democracy and a market economy.
But the overall picture has turned into a nightmare.
There is no money to pay wages or pensions, no cash to meet tax bills, and there are few ways for most people to buy the goods now cluttering the shelves of even the meanest shop.
"We have an economy without money," said museum director Stanislav Rybankov, complaining about the financial crisis facing all of Russia.
The cash shortages, stemming in part from a tight monetary policy brought in to crush inflation and meet the demands of the International Monetary Fund, have hit all Russian society.
Health workers demonstrate because they have not received their wages and army officers warn of trouble ahead.

"We've got to the stage where we can't keep quiet any more," said an unpaid doctor demonstrating outside the White House parliament building last week. "If we carry on like this we will be a dying nation."
Both life expectancy and birth rates are falling in the new Russia, partly because of rising poverty, partly because of insecurity about what will happen in the country now.
Government officials say the root of the cash problem lies in Russia's dismal record of tax collection, and the shortage of tax revenues means that ministries cannot pay their bills.
Companies, including rich firms in the important energy sector, say they cannot pay because they have not been paid for deliveries made on behalf of the state.

An IMF team left Moscow last week without recommending giving Russia the latest tranche of a $10 billion, three-year loan. A statement from the Russian Central Bank said the IMF experts were unhappy with low tax collection.

The crisis has created an army of Russians struggling to survive without cash. They borrow from friends and shops or stand on the edge of the road to sell pots and pans which they receive in lieu of wages.
In the real army, which has received only a fraction of funds promised in the budget, suicide rates are rising and even Defence Minister Igor Rodionov has warned of a future crisis.

"Russia's leadership and society should know that the chronic lack of funds is taking the armed forces to the brink of undesirable, and even uncontrollable, developments," Rodionov, a proponent of reform to transform Russia's conscript force into a professional army, said last week.
Government actions to resolve the crisis centre on draconian efforts to rake in extra tax, and President Boris Yeltsin has set up a special tax commission to force firms to pay.
Bankruptcy proceedings have been launched against a handful of firms and officials are inspecting the books of other companies.

But some local officials, jealous of their own regional autonomy, are determined to protect jobs and prevent the closure of major factories. The head of the autonomous region of Tatarstan has said the campaign was doomed.

"A feverish struggle for taxes and vain attempts to collect them remind us of the stagnation (the last years of the communist regime)," Tatarstan leader Mintimer Shaimiyev said, referring to Moscow's threats to launch bankruptcy proceedings against guilty firms.
"Now, as then, they are trying to get more milk from chronically undernourished cows."
